lead: A casting defect is a visible or measurable failure in a cast part. Its shape, size and location carry evidence: gas leaves round holes, shrinkage leaves rough cavities, and hot metal that stops early leaves a short edge. Foundries use this evidence to trace the cause to sand, pattern, gating, pouring or freezing, then change one variable and check the next batch. Rejection rate is money: every rejected casting has already consumed metal, melt energy and labour. The useful grouping is by cause: sand, pouring, freezing and pattern.
prereq: You need: 1.1 sand casting and moulding sand properties, 1.2 patterns, 1.4 gating and riser design, and 1.5 solidification; the mould, pattern, gating and freezing ideas explain most defects.

sections.h3: Read the defect before naming it

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this casting defects and remedies. A defect is not just a hole. The useful question is: what were the mould, metal, pattern and freezing doing when the hole formed? Read four clues. Position: top cope, bottom drag, gate, riser or core. Surface: smooth, rough, dendritic, oxidised or sandy. Shape: round, elongated, step or seam. Time: during pouring, during freezing, or after removal. A smooth round cavity high in the cope points to gas trapped by sand. A rough cavity at a thick section points to liquid shrinkage. A short, rounded edge points to metal that froze before filling. A crack with oxidised faces formed while the casting was hot. Visual and dimensional checks come first; dye penetrant finds surface-breaking cracks, while radiography and ultrasonic testing find internal defects. All of these belong to later non-destructive testing study. Record the casting number, mould number, pouring temperature and time. One defect is an anecdote; a pattern of ten is evidence.

sections.h3: Group by cause, then correct one variable

blocks.text: The figure groups the common defects into four families. Sand defects come from mould strength, moisture and ramming: blowhole, sand inclusion, scab, drop, penetration and swell. Pouring defects come from metal temperature, speed and cleanliness: misrun, cold shut, slag inclusion and runout. Freezing defects come from feeding and contraction: shrinkage cavity, hot tear and gas porosity. Gas porosity sits between the sand and freezing families; it is listed under freezing because the gas escapes during solidification. Pattern defects come from geometry alignment: mismatch and core shift. The figure shows one example from each family, not the full list. Treat the family as a hypothesis, not a verdict. A round hole can be a blowhole from damp sand or a gas pinhole from dissolved hydrogen; the location and metal grade separate them. A rough cavity in a thick hub is a shrinkage cavity; adding a riser changes the freezing order. Hot tears need a collapsible mould, not a slower pour. Change one variable, make a trial batch, and record the rejection rate. This closed loop is the foundry version of debug and test.

figure.caption: The tree groups defects by main cause; the first branch is sand, and a blowhole is its gas example. Notice that a defect name alone is weak evidence until the cause family is known.

examples.question: A foundry makes 500 castings in a shift. 35 are rejected. Find the rejection rate and the yield of good castings.
steps: Yield of good castings = (465 ÷ 500) × 100 = 93%, which is also 100% - 7% = 93%.
examples.answer: The rejection rate is 7% and the yield of good castings is 93%.
examples.check:
total = 500
rejected = 35
good = total - rejected
rejection_rate = rejected / total * 100
good_yield = good / total * 100
print(rejection_rate)
print(good_yield)

traps: A shrinkage cavity is rough and dendritic inside; a blowhole is smooth and round. Do not call every hole porosity.
A hot tear forms while the casting is hot and contracting, not after it is cold; a cold crack has a different history.
Misrun is incomplete filling; cold shut is two streams meeting without fusion. Both can look like a short edge or seam, but the cause and remedy differ.
Sand inclusion is loose sand; slag inclusion is slag. Slag often lies near the gate and is dark and glassy; sand is gritty.
Yield of good castings is not the same as casting yield (casting weight divided by poured metal weight). Read what the question asks.

quiz.q: Name two gas defects and one shrinkage defect.
quiz.a: Blowhole and porosity are gas defects; shrinkage cavity is a shrinkage defect.

quiz.q: Why does a hot tear form while the casting is still hot?
quiz.a: The casting is weak at high temperature. Contraction is blocked by a strong mould or core, so tensile strain exceeds the hot ductility and a tear opens.

quiz.q: A foundry makes 800 castings and rejects 48. Find the rejection rate and the yield of good castings.
A casting shows a smooth round hole at the top of the cope, and another casting shows a rough cavity in a thick hub. Identify each defect and give one remedy.
quiz.a: Smooth round hole high in the cope: blowhole from gas in sand; dry and vent the sand. Rough cavity in a thick hub: shrinkage cavity; add or enlarge a riser and place a chill.
Misrun: metal freezes before filling a section. Cold shut: two metal streams meet but do not fuse, leaving a rounded seam.

quiz.q: A casting shows sand inclusion and penetration. Which sand properties should be improved?
quiz.a: Sand inclusion means loose sand; penetration means metal entered sand gaps. Use stronger, finer sand, better ramming, lower moisture and a mould wash.
Mismatch is a cope and drag offset at the parting line. Core shift is movement of the core, making wall thickness uneven.

beyond: Not for the exam. Foundries track defects with Pareto charts, so the few causes that produce most rejections get fixed first. Casting simulation software predicts hot spots, air entrapment and hot tearing before a pattern is cut. Automotive and pump foundries use X-ray and computed tomography to inspect safety-critical castings. Search for casting defect atlas, hot tearing index, and feeding distance rules if you want the research view.
